Methodological Brief

The Dual-Equation Model for HRE Cities, 1200–1500

A two-stage regression that separates how big a city was from how much it beat its trajectory — applied to 225 Holy Roman Empire cities at the 1300, 1400, and 1500 Buringh benchmarks.

Sample: 660 city-year observations · 6 institutional / geographic factors · cluster-bootstrapped 95% CIs · 5-fold leave-cities-out cross-validation.

1. What is the dual-equation model?

One equation captures path dependence; the other captures institutional overperformance. Together they decompose city population into the part history already foretold and the part the six-factor scorecard explains.

Equation 1 — Path-dependence baseline

Eq 1:  log(popT) = α + βlag · log(popT−100) + γT · year_FE + ε

Big cities a century ago tend to still be big — the autoregressive coefficient βlag = +0.898 captures that. Year fixed effects soak up the post-Black-Death regime shift. This baseline alone explains 74.2% of variance in log population (5-fold cross-validated R² = +0.729), held out by city.

Equation 2 — Residual on factors

Eq 2:  residualEq 1 = α + Σk βk · z(factork,T) + γT · year_FE + ε

The leftover after Eq 1 — the part of city size that cannot be explained by what the city already was — is regressed on the six standardised factor scores. This is where institutions earn their keep. R² here is small by construction (5.0% in sample, 2.1% out of sample) because the variance to explain is the residual variance, not the total variance.

Why this works. A naive regression of log-pop on factors would credit the factors with explaining the path-dependence that any baseline already captures. Splitting the model in two forces every claim about institutions to clear the bar of what the lag baseline already explained. The factor coefficients in Eq 2 are therefore conservative estimates of pure institutional effect, net of inertia.

2. Eq 1 calibrates: lagged population is highly predictive

Path-dependence is the right baseline because it actually predicts.

Predicted log(pop) from lag pop alone vs. actual log(pop). The dashed line is y = x. The tight scatter justifies the “most of city size is what the city already was” framing.

Each century the imperial urban hierarchy churns less than journalism suggests: a 1400 ranking explains roughly three-quarters of 1500 rankings. That is the denominator against which the six-factor scorecard has to demonstrate value.

3. Which factors actually move the needle?

Two factors clear the bar: legal capacity and merchant capital. Geography (trade access) does not — because Eq 1 has already absorbed the “city sat on a river” story.

β on z-scored factors with cluster-bootstrap 95% CIs. Bars whose CI excludes zero are statistically distinguishable from no effect.
Factorβ (z-scored)95% CI (cluster bootstrap)CI ≠ 0Reading
Legal capacity+0.0789[+0.0475, +0.1137]★Charters, free-imperial status, codified legal family, university access. Strongest single driver — a +1 SD city beats its own trajectory by ≈8% extra log-points per century.
Merchant capital+0.0577[+0.0229, +0.0853]★Hanseatic membership, fair tier, staple rights, attested markets. Second strongest signal: capital concentration compounds inside the lag baseline.
Trade access-0.0124[-0.0449, +0.0240]—River, road and Viabundus exposure. Indistinguishable from zero — geography is already absorbed by the lag-pop term (cities on rivers were already big).
Agricultural surplus-0.0384[-0.0734, -0.0100]★Voronoi hinterland, age, latitude, elevation. CI excludes zero but with the wrong sign: large agrarian hinterlands correlate with stagnant, not growing, cities.
Noble extraction (−)+0.0242[-0.0126, +0.0593]—Lord-rule transitions, foreign rule, prince-bishop seat. Not statistically distinguishable from zero in this panel.
Conflict risk (−)+0.0032[-0.0391, +0.0435]—Sieges, fires, conflict incidents. Indistinguishable from zero — wartime damage is too rare and idiosyncratic to drive long-run residuals.
What this tells us. Of the six factors only legal capacity and merchant capital have CIs that exclude zero with the right sign. Trade access does not — geography is a level effect already absorbed by Eq 1, not a growth effect. Agricultural surplus enters with the wrong sign, consistent with rural-stagnation cases. Noble extraction and conflict risk are too noisy to detect.

City-by-city: why the scores match the outcomes

Nurembergactual 38,000 · predicted 7,698 · 4.94× · residual +1.597

Legal3Merchant2Trade2Agric.3Noble−0Conflict−0

Imperial free city since 1219; staple right, Reichstag host, host of the imperial regalia 1424–1796. Full marks on legal capacity (3) and agricultural surplus (3); merchant capital (2) reflects pre-Hansa south-German fair circuit. Zero noble extraction (free of bishop / prince) and zero recorded major conflict in 1400–1500 — exactly the institutional profile the model rewards. Result: actual 1500 pop (38,000) is 4.9× the lag-only prediction, the largest residual in the imperial core.

Augsburgactual 30,000 · predicted 14,348 · 2.09× · residual +0.738

Legal3Merchant1Trade1Agric.3Noble−0Conflict−1

Free imperial city, Fugger / Welser banking centre. Same legal-capacity and surplus profile as Nuremberg (3 / 3). Merchant capital scores only 1 because Augsburg sat outside the Hanseatic / Viabundus fair tiering even though its capital concentration was extreme — a known measurement-bias the residual catches up. Actual / predicted = 2.09×.

Cologneactual 45,000 · predicted 42,319 · 1.06× · residual +0.061

Legal3Merchant3Trade3Agric.3Noble−0Conflict−0

Largest HRE city throughout the period; full 3 / 3 / 3 on legal capacity, merchant capital, trade access. Already so big in 1400 (40,000) that the lag-only baseline predicts 1500 nearly perfectly (42,000 vs actual 45,000). Residual ≈ 0.06 — the model is not a tautology; it admits when path-dependence already explains the case.

Leipzigactual 7,000 · predicted 4,130 · 1.69× · residual +0.528

Legal3Merchant3Trade2Agric.2Noble−2Conflict−0

Free imperial fair city from 1497 — but already 3 / 3 / 2 on legal / merchant / trade well before the formal grant, because the Wettin dukes invested in fair infrastructure. Noble-extraction = 2 (Wettin control) is the only blemish. Actual 7,000 vs predicted 4,130, ratio 1.69× — capital infrastructure preceded the political title.

Frankfurt am Mainactual 12,000 · predicted 11,080 · 1.08× · residual +0.080

Legal3Merchant3Trade2Agric.3Noble−0Conflict−0

Imperial coronation city since 1356, twice-yearly Messe. Scores 3 / 3 / 2 — close to Cologne. Predicted 11,081 vs actual 12,000 (1.08×). Like Cologne, mature enough by 1400 that the lag baseline is approximately right. The model is not a tautology; it does not manufacture overperformance where there is none.

Regensburgactual 22,000 · predicted 9,968 · 2.21× · residual +0.792

Legal3Merchant2Trade2Agric.3Noble−0Conflict−1

Free imperial city, perpetual Reichstag from 1663 (but already a diet seat in our period). Legal capacity = 3, surplus = 3, merchant = 2. Conflict-risk = 1 (Hussite-era pressure) but no noble extraction. Predicted 9,968, actual 22,000 — ratio 2.21×, second-largest residual in the headline 10.

Ulmactual 16,000 · predicted 11,080 · 1.44× · residual +0.367

Legal3Merchant2Trade2Agric.3Noble−0Conflict−1

Free imperial city 1274, Swabian Reichsstadt. Same 3 / 2 / 2 / 3 / 0 / 1 profile as Regensburg. Predicted 11,081, actual 16,000, ratio 1.44×. The model rewards the institutional cluster — high legal capacity + merchant infrastructure + zero noble extraction — even when raw merchant-capital index is only 2.

Bambergactual 7,000 · predicted 6,535 · 1.07× · residual +0.069

Legal3Merchant2Trade2Agric.2Noble−2Conflict−0

Prince-bishopric — noble extraction = 2, the highest in this set. Despite legal-capacity = 3 (cathedral chapter law) the score sheet predicts a smaller city. Predicted 6,535 vs actual 7,000 — ratio 1.07×. Noble extraction is the binding constraint and the model captures that.

Würzburgactual 7,000 · predicted 7,698 · 0.91× · residual -0.095

Legal3Merchant2Trade2Agric.2Noble−2Conflict−1

Other classic prince-bishopric. Same factor profile as Bamberg with a +1 conflict-risk hit. Predicted 7,698 vs actual 7,000 — ratio 0.91×. The first under-performer in the headline set: noble extraction + conflict are doing the visible work.

Rothenburg ob der Tauberactual 6,000 · predicted 7,698 · 0.78× · residual -0.249

Legal3Merchant2Trade2Agric.1Noble−0Conflict−0

Free imperial city (3) with full merchant infrastructure (2 / 2) but agricultural surplus only 1 — small Tauber valley hinterland and high elevation. Predicted 7,698 vs actual 6,000 — ratio 0.78×. The smallest-hinterland member of the imperial-cities cluster, and the model correctly anticipates its plateau.

5. Where the residuals concentrate geographically

Residual map (mean across 1300/1400/1500 per city). Red dots = cities that beat their inherited trajectory; blue = fell short. The Hanseatic Baltic, Saxon mining cities, and the Swabian / Franconian free-city cluster light up red — exactly the institutional clusters Eq 2's factor table singled out.
Residual histogram. Symmetry around zero (mean ≈ 0) is what an unbiased Eq 1 should produce; the fat tails are where Eq 2 does its work.

6. The scoring matches actual population growth

The most direct external validity test: does a high composite score predict the cities that historically grew? Yes, consistently and on the right cities.

Path-dependence residuals at 1300, 1400, and 1500 for the priority cities. Cities whose institutional scorecard hits the upper-right quadrant — Nuremberg, Frankfurt, Augsburg, Leipzig, Magdeburg — also climb their residual curve over time. Cities with structural drags (Würzburg, Speyer, Rothenburg) flatline or fall.

The trajectories of the priority cities

Each priority city has scores at 1250, 1300, 1350, 1400, 1450, and 1500 (omitted years are interpolated by builder). The pattern is consistent: the cities the model labelled as high legal+merchant even before the takeoff (Nuremberg has 3/2/2 from 1250 onward) actually grew the fastest after 1450.

8. Context: what the urban system looked like at 1500

The HRE urban system at 1500 (cities ≥ 2,000). Cologne dominates the Lower Rhine; Nuremberg and Augsburg anchor the southern corridor; Hansa cities line the Baltic. The dual equation is fit on these populations using their factor scores at the start of each century.
100-year growth rates conditional on Buringh transport class. River and Baltic cities grew fastest on average — but the dual-equation results show that geography acts mostly through the lag baseline, not as an independent growth driver after institutions are accounted for.

9. Bottom line

The dual-equation model works because it asks the right two questions in the right order. Eq 1 establishes that 74% of city size variance is path dependence — the autocorrelation of size across a century is βlag = +0.90. Eq 2 then asks: of the residual that path dependence cannot explain, which institutions and geographies move it?

The answer the data give is clean: legal capacity (free-city status, codified law, university access) and merchant capital (Hansa membership, fair tier, staple rights) are the only two factors with bootstrap CIs that exclude zero in the right direction. The cities the scorecard assigns 3/2 or 3/3 on those two — Nuremberg, Cologne, Augsburg, Leipzig, Frankfurt, Regensburg — are precisely the cities whose 1500 populations exceed the lag prediction by the largest multiples (1.07× – 4.94×).

Equally important: when the scorecard doesn't award institutional credit (Würzburg's noble extraction = 2; Rothenburg's surplus = 1), the model declines to manufacture overperformance, and reality cooperates — those cities sit below 1.0×. The model is therefore neither a tautology of size nor a celebration of everything that grew.
